anchor: `security.allow_internal_targets` (default `false`) controls whether the scanners that fetch a URL, namely the JWT/JWKS, OpenAPI spec and SAML metadata probes and the REST fuzzer, may contact internal and loopback addresses (RFC1918 ranges, `127.x.x.x`, link-local). A URL on the cloud-metadata address `169.254.169.254` is still refused when it is `true`. The dashboard reads this flag from the server's own config file (`QUIRK_CONFIG_PATH`, default `./config.yaml`) and copies it into each job it dispatches; a browser cannot set it. The CLI equivalent is `--allow-internal-targets`. It does **not** restrict which targets you can scan: the core TLS, SSH and fingerprint scans, and the dashboard's New Scan form, accept loopback and RFC1918 targets either way.

anchor: The QUIRK dashboard (served by `quirk serve`) optionally enforces token-based authentication on its `/api/*` routes, with two exceptions: `GET /api/health` and `GET /api/config` are always open (the login page needs them before a token exists). `POST /api/sensor/push` is separate: it always requires a per-sensor token and does not accept the dashboard token. Authentication is **off by default** — an empty or absent `security.api_token` means the dashboard is accessible without credentials (suitable for local development only). `quirk serve` refuses to bind a network-reachable host without a token unless you pass `--insecure`.

anchor: Run `quirk token generate --config config.yaml` to write a random token into this field. Once the token is non-empty, the dashboard requires authentication on every `/api/*` request except the two open routes above. The dashboard reads the YAML token from the file named by `QUIRK_CONFIG_PATH` (default `./config.yaml` in the server's working directory), not from the `--config` you gave `quirk token`, so make sure both name the same file. An absent or empty file means authentication is off. A token in the file enables authentication even when the file holds only a `security:` section. A file that exists but cannot be read or parsed (malformed YAML, or a top level or `security` entry that is not a mapping) stops `quirk serve` with exit code 2 and makes every protected `/api/*` route answer 503 (`DASHBOARD-014`) until the file is fixed. For production deployments, set `QUIRK_API_TOKEN`.

Baseline text: **`match_confidence` is not the same field as the pre-existing `confidence` column.** `confidence` (used elsewhere in hardware fingerprinting, e.g. §9.5's CVE correlation) describes confidence in a *probe result* — how sure QUIRK is about a parsed vendor/model/firmware value. `match_confidence` describes confidence in *cross-scan device identity* — how sure QUIRK is that two rows scanned at different times represent the same physical device. fix: Was: '**Where to look when PLCs stop being fingerprinted.** If Modbus/BACnet devices that used to appear in scheduled-scan results stop showing up, check the scheduler's log output for a line matching this shape: ``` OT/ICS probing suppressed for schedule 'nightly-plant-scan' (cron='0 * * * *'): removed keys ('enable_modbus', 'enable_bacnet') — reason: ... ``` The literal text `OT/ICS probing suppressed` always appears, followed by the schedule name, the exact keys that were stripped from the generated config, and the reason (cadence-floor violation or the recurring opt-in being off). The sample showed a tuple and '...' where the code prints a list and a literal reason; and the line is logged at INFO with no handler configured anywhere, so it is never printed by default (probe: 0 bytes on stderr). Pointed operators at the generated config, which always records the strip, and stated the logging caveat. Product follow-up: todo 261013-doc224-otics-suppression-log-line-never-printed.

claim: ticket fingerprints come from a normalized title (compute_fingerprint via normalize_finding_title); before Phase 178 (5.18.0 and earlier) they hashed the raw title; normalization drops the label/version in five container-image titles (End-of-life <label> in container image; Severely outdated / Outdated Python cryptography package (<version>); Outdated pyOpenSSL package (<version>); Outdated libgcrypt (<version>)); the table also maps the dashboard's 'Certificate expiring in {N} day(s)' title, but quirk ticket create reads findings-*.json whose cert-expiry title 'TLS certificate expiring within 30 days' never carried a day count | covers: Finding fingerprints — the dedup key used to decide "have I already opened a ticket for this" — ;; are now computed from a **normalized** title (`quirk/ticketing/base.py::compute_fingerprint`, ;; routed through `quirk.compliance.normalize_finding_title`). Before Phase 178 (5.18.0 and earlier), ;; the fingerprint hashed the raw title text. The normalization drops the label or version that five ;; container-image finding titles interpolate: `End-of-life <label> in container image`, ;; `Severely outdated Python cryptography package (<version>) in container image`, ;; `Outdated Python cryptography package (<version>) in container image`, ;; `Outdated pyOpenSSL package (<version>) in container image`, and ;; `Outdated libgcrypt (<version>) in container image`. fix: Was: 'Finding fingerprints — the dedup key used to decide "have I already opened a ticket for this" — are now computed from a **normalized** title (`quirk/ticketing/base.py::compute_fingerprint`, routed through `quirk.compliance.normalize_finding_title`). Before Phase 178, the fingerprint hashed the raw title text, and one finding family interpolates a changing value into that title: `"Certificate expiring in {N} day(s)"`, where `N` counts down every day. That meant a still-open certificate-expiry finding minted a brand-new fingerprint — and therefore a brand-new Jira issue or ServiceNow incident — on every single scan, instead of being recognized as the same finding it was yesterday. **The only affected family is certificate-expiry findings.** No other finding title changed its fingerprint-relevant classification in this phase.'. `quirk ticket create` fingerprints the scan's findings-*.json, whose cert-expiry title is the constant 'TLS certificate expiring within 30 days' (also in v5.18.0); 'Certificate expiring in {N} day(s)' is a dashboard-only title. The families that actually re-keyed against v5.18.0's raw-title formula are the five container-image titles inherited from TITLE_PREFIX_ALIASES. Rewrote 14.1 to name them. section: ## 15. Remediation Tracking Scope (first released in 5.19.0 — Phase 179)
claim: not_observed is persisted and is every finding's starting state; a finding is never inferred closed from absence; a detected finding keeps not_observed (nothing promotes it to open), so not_observed means not verified closed, covering both found again and not checked | covers: - **`not_observed` is a real, persisted state, and it is the state every finding starts in.** A ;; finding is never inferred `closed` from absence. But in this release `not_observed` is also ;; the state a finding keeps when the scan *detected* it: nothing promotes a detected finding to ;; `open` (see §16, "The four states"). So `not_observed` means "not verified closed", which covers ;; both "found again this scan" and "not checked this run" (a narrower port scope, a disabled ;; connector, an unreachable host). Never read it as "there's nothing there", and do not read it ;; as "we did not check" either; use the scan's findings list to tell the two apart.

fix: Was: '- **`not_observed` is a real, persisted third state — distinct from both `open` and `closed`.** An item this scan did not see evidence for is recorded as `not_observed`, never inferred as `closed`. A report reading "9 closed, 4 open, 12 not observed" is telling you something true and useful: those 12 were not verified this scan, one way or the other. anchor: `ITEM_STATES` in `quirk/intelligence/remediation.py` defines four closure states. In this
claim: ITEM_STATES defines four states but only three are written: not_observed (every detected finding, never moved to open), closed (written to the earlier scan's record when the current scan rechecked the host:port healthily and did not find it; the current scan's burndown and badges never count it), resurfaced (current record of a finding whose latest earlier record is closed; open-like, reported separately, history retained); open is never written so every open count is 0 | covers: `ITEM_STATES` in `quirk/intelligence/remediation.py` defines four closure states. In this ;; release only three of them are ever written, and they are written to different scans' records: ;; - **`not_observed`** — every finding a scan detects is recorded in this state ;; (`DEFAULT_ITEM_STATE`), and nothing later moves a still-present finding to `open`. It also ;; stays the state of anything the scan could not verify (see the troubleshooting list below). ;; - **`closed`** — written to the **earlier** scan's record of a finding, when that finding was ;; present in a comparable prior scan and the current scan positively rechecked the same host:port ;; with a healthy probe and did not find it. The current scan has no record of a finding it did not ;; find, so the current scan's burndown and roadmap badges never count it as closed; the closure is ;; kept on the prior scan's record and in the closure event log. ;; - **`resurfaced`** — written to the current scan's record when a finding whose most recent earlier ;; record is `closed` is detected again. It is counted as open-like for reporting, but reported as ;; its own line rather than folded into `open`, and its closure history is retained. ;; - **`open`** — defined, but no code path writes it, so every `open` count is 0. ;; Plaintext HTTP findings can never close. The scan raises them on endpoints whose protocol is ;; `HTTP`, no probe family claims that protocol, and so the probe-health check for that host:port ;; always reads `not_run`. ;; **Absence alone never closes an item.** A host that stops appearing in a scan — because it was ;; decommissioned, because the target list shrank, because a segment of the network was unreachable — ;; is not evidence anything was fixed. Closure requires the current scan to have positively rechecked
